headline.main: Katya, Ira and Zhenya Take on Putin: The Difficulties of Protesting the War in Russia
headline.social: Katya, Ira and Zhenya Take on Putin: The Difficulties of Protesting the War in Russia

intro: Who still dares to protest the war in Russia? Women. They hold up signs, lay flowers, hide messages in books and write to political prisoners. DER SPIEGEL spent months following three of them.
text:
Just a few more minutes, says Katya. She is standing in front of a monument to the victims of Stalin in northern Moscow and holding up a sign: "Freedom for the political prisoners.” In her other hand are two red roses. Those who still do such a thing in today’s Russia know full well that they are risking arrest.
Two passersby glance over at the dainty woman. A prisoner transport van, siren blaring, speeds past in the evening rush-hour traffic on the multi-lane ring road. A companion takes photos of Katya, which she will later post on Facebook. The police could show up at any moment and take her away. Her lawyer has warned her that if she gets caught one more time, she will likely be thrown in prison. A woman in her late 40s, Katya has been levied fines on seven occasions for protesting against the war in Ukraine – or for "discrediting” the army, as it is officially called.
After 10 minutes, she puts down her sign, grabs her backpack and walks to the subway. A butterfly in the Ukrainian national colors of blue and yellow dangles from her bag next to a colorful peace symbol and the crossed-out English word "War.” Katya could get in trouble for this bag alone: Three additional "discreditations.”
Vladimir Putin’s war against his neighboring country has now been underway for almost three years, bombing cities and killing civilians. During this time, Russian security agencies have almost completely cleared the country’s streets of those who actively oppose the war. Public space is reserved exclusively for tales of battlefield heroes and their triumphs.
Shortly after ordering the invasion of Ukraine, Putin issued two harsh censorship laws. One of them targeted alleged acts of "discrediting the Russian armed forces,” and the other aimed at the "public dissemination of knowingly false information” about the military’s deployment. Those who call the war what it is, or who openly criticize the invasion face severe penalties of up to 15 years in prison.
In May of last year, when Putin had himself installed in office for a fifth term, he said: "We are a unified and great nation. Together, we will be victorious.” It was a message to the entire state apparatus, from the office of the presidency, the security agencies and the ministries, on down to the media and state-run companies, and even to regional administrations, universities, schools and kindergartens: The president demands unconditional loyalty. Those who publicly question the war and Putin’s course are criminalized.
The Russian human rights organization OVD-Info lists over 20,000 arrests made due to anti-war protests, including a striking number of women. It used to be the case that large demonstrations primarily attracted young men. But the activists from OVD-Info have determined that women have made up almost half of those arrested at such protests since the beginning of the year. Their share was even 70 percent during demonstrations against Putin’s mobilization in September 2022. Men who were arrested risked being conscripted into the army and sent to the front. OVD-Info has documented several such cases.
As such, Katya believes, it is less dangerous for women to demonstrate. "But they also realized more quickly what this war means: all of the deaths, the human suffering, the millions of refugees.” To protect her safety, she has requested that her full name not be used in this article. She is one of three women protesters who DER SPIEGEL has followed over the course of several months – women who continue to engage in acts of defiance despite the dangers.
Katya says she is afraid. "But I can’t sit at home and remain silent. That would drive me crazy.”
So she heads out onto the street, driven to desperation by the indifference shown by so many others. Every day, Russian rockets and drones are killing Ukrainians, she says. Every day, the Russian regime is locking away more political prisoners. Some of them have starved themselves to death in prison, like the anti-war activist Pavel Kushnir in late July last year. And most Russians, she says, simply don’t care.
"For the first time in my life, I feel rage,” Katya says.
In the evenings, she says during a meeting near the memorial to the Ukrainian poet Lesya Ukrainka, she sometimes just sits there, not knowing what she should write to her Ukrainian friends. She has chosen her seat in the café so she can look out at the statue.
Before heading to the café, Katya placed carnations on the base of the statue, something she does regularly. The first time she brought flowers to "Lesya” was in January 2023, together with two other women. A Russian ballistic missile had just struck a residential building in Dnipro, killing 46 and injuring at least 80. The carnations were just a small gesture of public sympathy, one which dozens of Muscovites joined within a few days after seeing images of the event on social media. They transformed "Lesya” into an improvised memorial.
Police officers took up positions and began arresting those who sought to display images of the destroyed building. And city workers began regularly clearing away the roses and chrysanthemums from the statue’s granite pedestal. Flowers had become political.
Katya is ashamed by the war. Sometimes, she posts a black image with the names of recently bombed Ukrainian cities to Facebook. She has adjusted her account settings so that only friends can see her posts. But who knows, she says.
Katya has been taken into temporary custody 10 times, and she has had to pay fines amounting to more than 200,000 rubles, the equivalent of almost 2,000 euros. Supporters have given her donations so she can pay the fines and some of the penalties are already past the statute of limitations, but there have been too many.
"My children are likely protecting me from being sent to prison,” Katya believes. She and her husband have six sons, ranging in age from the seven-year-old twins to 16. She shows a photo of her and the kids, arms around each other on an early summer day standing in front of a monastery on the White Sea. From a purely legal standpoint, parents of minor children are not allowed to be locked up. But public officials in other parts of Russia don’t seem to care much about the letter of the law: Anti-war activists in the regions of Tula and Buryatia have been thrown in jail and their children put in homes.
Katya is the kind of mother that Putin is otherwise quite fond of showcasing: married, many children, a devout Christian and takes care of her aging mother, who lives together with them. She has a degree in child psychology, but she is largely a stay-home mother, aside from taking small jobs like cleaning, courier deliveries or accompanying sick children to school to earn a bit of extra money for the family. Putin, who poses as a proponent of conservative values, has been presenting awards to the parents of multi-child families for years.
But she won’t be receiving an award from him, says Katya with a laugh. She looks out the window of the café. Her carnations are still lying at "Lesya’s” feet.
Women like her are considered traitors in Russia. Her mother, a Putin supporter, even criticizes her at home. She once accused Katya of being a "fascist,” she says quietly, because of her support for the purported Nazis in Ukraine. It is painful, she says, to hear her mother parrot the things she hears on internet programs from prominent propagandists like Vladimir Solovyov and Margarita Simonyan.
Since then, they only speak about day-to-day concerns: the children, school, food. Things aren’t easy with her husband either, she says. He believes that the U.S. is to be blamed for the war, that Washington provoked it. It’s pointless, she says, to talk to him about it. But he does support her, she says, sometimes accompanying her to "Lesya” and he has also spent hours with her at the police station.
Katya’s telephone rings. Her face brightens; it’s one of her sons. "Have you done your homework, math and reading my sunshine? Good, then you can play video games. I’ll be there in an hour.”
The rights of women in Russia have been continually curtailed since the beginning of the war. Clinics refuse to perform abortions and those who don’t want to have children are not allowed to speak about their choice in public. Violence in families is a taboo subject, particularly when traumatized soldiers tyrannize family members. The country has no laws protecting women from domestic violence. One group that is raising awareness of the problem on social media channels is Feminist Anti-War Resistance, known as Feministskoye antivoyennoye soprotivleniye (FAS) in Russian. The group published an anti-war manifesto just a few hours after Putin issued the order to invade Ukraine.
The group is organized decentrally in many different regions of Russia and there are no hierarchies. The women remain anonymous and exchange information in encrypted chats.
Ira, who is in her early 20s and is an activist with FAS, has asked that her real name not be used for reasons of safety.
In the first year of the war, she roamed through her neighborhood putting up anti-war posters on the walls. In the second year, she only dared to visit the dead, with security cameras being less prominent in cemeteries than in the city. In Moscow, many of the surveillance cameras are outfitted with facial recognition technology, and the police have used it on many occasions to identify and arrest anti-war activists.
On a snowy Sunday in October 2023, Ira walks through the gate of Vvedenskoye Cemetery in eastern Moscow and continues deep into the maze of narrow paths and gravestones. Only very few others are wandering through the 18th century site with its mausoleums and tall trees. After a few hundred meters, Ira stops at a randomly chosen family grave. Next to it is a large, faded teddy bear, an indicator that a child is also buried here.
Ira looks around slowly and pulls a poster out of her shoulder bag. On it, she has written in black and red letters: "The village Hrosa. A Russian missile killed 52 peaceable residents. Shame! Come to your senses!” She leans it against the bear. A few days earlier, a Russian Iskander-M missile had detonated in the village in northeast Ukraine.
Ira continues her walk, ultimately setting up four posters bearing anti-war verses from well-known artists on various graves. One of them describes the senselessness of World War I. "If just one person thinks about one of my posters,” she says, "I will have achieved something.”
A few months later, in 2024, the third year of the war, Ira has become even more cautious. In April, the Justice Ministry declared Feminist Anti-War Resistance to be an "undesirable organization.” It is now banned in Russia. Those who continue working with it face possible prison time. "At least we weren’t branded extremists,” says Ira sarcastically – like the Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny and those who work for him. When asked how she is doing, she replies dryly: "I’m alive.”
In surveys, people living in authoritarian countries often say what they believe is expected of them, making it difficult to determine the true mood of the Russian population. Sociologist Lev Gudkov, from the country’s only independent public opinion research institute Levada, has his staff speak personally with people, not over the phone. He believes doing so gives him a clearer view of the situation. He says that around 44 percent of Russians openly support the war of aggression with 7 percent explicitly opposed. Many simply accept the campaign.
Well-heeled Muscovites are particularly pragmatic about the war and have come to terms with it and with Putin’s shift away from the West. They get their iPhones through intermediary countries now that they can no longer be purchased in Russia because of the sanctions. And instead of making trips to Paris or London, they travel into the broad expanse of Siberia or to "friendly foreign countries” like the United Arab Emirates, Vietnam, Thailand or Turkey. Others just avoid all the "negativity” associated with the war and politics and focus on yoga or running marathons.
Ira says that she’s only doing "little things” now and is no longer trying to reach those who support the war or who are indifferent to it.
In a café in the heart of Moscow, she grabs a coffee at the counter along with two novels available to guests – a service that some cafés offer. At one of the tables in the back, Ira opens the first book and quickly shoves a piece of paper bearing a hand-drawn peace dove into it. She looks up, leafs further through the pages at sticks a second piece of paper into the book on which she has written in blue ballpoint pen: "You aren’t the only one who is opposed to what is happening.” Further back, between pages 434 and 435, she inserts another message: "Peace will come.” She then closes "Oblomov,” the classic by Ivan Goncharov, and glances around the room.
Two tables to Ira’s right, a man and a woman are chatting away. To her left, a woman is typing concentratedly on her laptop. Up front, a man with a coffee is staring out the window. Ira takes a sip from her cup, puts the two novels back and leaves the café.
She doesn’t consider herself brave. "What I am doing is the absolute moral minimum.”
A lot of things are now taking place underground, says Ira. Activists hold security training sessions on the internet, showing which messenger apps to use and which to avoid, how to hide your identity online and how to stay away from surveillance by Russian agencies, which are constantly increasing their efforts at controlling online communication. Only carefully selected and vetted guests are invited to readings. Ira is planning one on the subject of resistance.
The death of opposition leader Navalny, who died last February in a penal colony very likely as a result of poisoning, shocked her, says Ira. But it also gave her strength, because she saw how he brought together people from around the country. She says that almost 300 people registered with the FAS within one week. "We’re still there. We can still do something.”
Huge billboards have been erected at important intersections and along major arterials in Moscow; posters of heroes hang at bus stops. They all show the faces of soldiers next to the message: "Russia’s pride.” Zhenya, a 21-year-old university student, spent quite some time pasting black-and-white stickers reading "No to War” on lampposts and the walls of buildings. She tried to place them as high up as possible to make them more difficult to remove. She says she did so to remind people that there were still opponents to the war.
But then, she was taken into police custody. She was standing outside a Moscow courthouse during a political trial, and she yelled out "Shame!” when the verdict was announced. She was immediately led away.
"Just 15 days arrest,” Zhenya says with a dismissive wave during a walk through a park in northern Moscow. "Laughable,” she says, in comparison with the many years behind bars that the country’s estimated 800 political prisoners must endure.
She walks rapidly around a pond. Zhenya, too, has asked that she remain anonymous for her own safety. She circles the pond once, twice, three times before then saying: "As Russians, we have to take responsibility for what has happened.”
She has continued her activities, but no longer with stickers. After her arrest, the police visited her twice at home, she says, making it dangerous to keep stickers there. She now wants to do what she can to help those who have paid for their acts of protest with their freedom. Once a month, she organizes an evening event where Muscovites can write letters to political prisoners. It is important, she says, to show those in prison that they have not been forgotten. Letters or postcards, she says, are often the only connection these people have to the outside world.
Because she wants their solidarity with the prisoners to be visible, the meetings are held in cafés. One time, café workers asked them not to come back, saying the owner was worried about potential problems with the authorities. And it’s not difficult for them to find excuses for such problems: alleged violations of fire protection regulations, for example, or even a tax audit.
At least she hasn’t yet been reported to the police, says Zhenya. Denunciations have become commonplace in Russia, she says; you never know who is sitting next to you and listening in. In the city of Khabarovsk far to the east, police took the step of temporarily detaining an organizer of such a letter-writing evening without saying why. Writing to prisoners is not prohibited in Russia, but it also isn’t free of risk.
In the "Open Room” in Moscow, a meetup for activists and also a place frequently visited by the police, Zhenya and other women on a Saturday evening are distributing felt-tip pens, ballpoints, scissors, stickers, paper, envelopes and stamps among the tables. Photos of political prisoners hang on the walls, people like Navalny and the Moscow District Council deputy Alexei Gorinov. There are a couple of gaps among the pictures: Until early August, photos of the Kremlin critics Ilya Yashin and Vladimir Kara-Mursa were also on display, but the two were then released as part of a prisoner exchange with Germany and other Western countries.
Almost 30 men and women drop by in the ensuing hours. Zhenya shows them QR codes with links to human rights organizations that maintain lists of the prisoners and tells them things they should avoid writing so that their letters make it through the prison censors. "Ask nothing about the prisoner’s case and don’t write anything in a foreign language.” Instead, letter-writers should simply relate something from their daily lives. "Or maybe a poem,” she says. A young man puts stickers of trees on his letter and a woman draws a cat in the margin because she knows the prisoner likes them.
An older man from just outside Moscow is here for the first time. He asks Zhenya to put her own address on the stamped return envelope. He is afraid that his letter might attract unwanted attention from the security authorities.
In this third year of the war, Zhenya and Ira seem more determined. The women have decided to remain in Russia, to ride it out.
"If I was to leave the country,” says Zhenya, "I would be leaving those in the lurch who are worse off than me.”
Ira says: "The regime is growing stronger and stronger. We can’t change that. We can only adapt so that later, when an opportunity for change arises, we are ready.”
Katya, the mother of six sons, by contrast, seems exhausted. The first months of 2024 were hard, she says, with the police calling several times to ask where she and her children were. "They know full well that my children are my weak spot.” She and her family are not currently living at the address where they are registered.
At school, maps show the Russian border deep inside Ukraine, and the reference is consistently to the "special military operation,” as the war is still officially called, even in the third year. A mandatory subject for Katya’s 14-year-old son is "Defense of the Fatherland.” Every day in the subway, Katya sees the ads for contract soldiers flashing on the screens of the ticket machines. Men from Moscow are promised "5.2 million rubles in the first year,” the equivalent of 50,000 euros.
Katya’s oldest son will be required to register with the military authorities in a few months, like all young men. He will then no longer be allowed to leave the country. "I would never forgive myself for not saving my sons,” she says.
The Russian army has begun using the police to conscript young men by force. Katya’s husband and her mother don’t find it that bad that the children have to enroll in the military. "Our grandfathers fought against fascism, our grandchildren can do the same,” her mother said, says Katya, grimacing. She says she is having a hard time sleeping, with thoughts racing through her head.
Should she leave the country with the children? It is something that she, who considers herself a patriot, has never wanted to do. Would that make her a traitor? Would she be able to return to Russia later? What if she stays and is sent to prison? Who would take care of her six sons?
Katya spent weeks struggling with these questions before finally applying for a humanitarian visa in Germany for her family. She received help from an organization that provides political assistance to persecuted people.
All the while, she continued walking through Moscow with her backpack. Subway riders below the city streets would see the blue-and-yellow butterfly and quickly look down at the floor. On several occasions, Katya was insulted as an enemy of Russia by nationalist activists, and once, a stranger even filmed her. Sometimes, she would meet up with others like her, pleasant events despite everything. When yet another missile would strike yet another Ukrainian village, she would bring flowers to "Lesya.” Often, she sat alone on a bench at the statue.
In October, she was handed the visa for her and her family at the Consulate General. She teared up for a moment, she says.
In parting, just a few days before she left Russia at the end of the year, Katya said that it helped her to know that she was at least robbing Putin of her six sons. "Six fewer potential soldiers. That, too, is a form of protest.”
